items.name: Sun
facts: Holds 99.86 % of the solar system's mass.
Light from its surface takes about 8 min 20 s to reach Earth.
Its core fuses about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen every second.

items.name: Mercury
facts: A day from noon to noon lasts 176 Earth days, two of its years.
It spins three times for every two orbits: a 3:2 spin–orbit resonance.
Its iron core fills about 85 % of the planet's radius.
MESSENGER found water ice in permanently shadowed polar craters.

items.name: Venus
facts: Surface pressure is about 92 bar and the surface is about 465 °C.
It spins backwards, once every 243 days.
Its clouds are sulfuric acid; the cloud tops circle the planet in about 4 days (super-rotation).
Soviet Venera landers sent the only pictures from its surface (1975–1982).

items.name: Earth
facts: The only known world with liquid water on its surface and life.
The Moon slows its spin: the day grows longer by about 2 ms per century.
Getting to low orbit needs about 9.4 km/s of Δv, including losses to drag and gravity.

items.name: Moon
facts: It moves away from Earth by about 3.8 cm per year (laser ranging).
It always shows the same face: its spin is tidally locked to its orbit.
Shackleton crater, at the south pole, has a floor that never sees sunlight.
Twelve people walked on it, from Apollo 11 to Apollo 17 (1969–1972).

items.name: Mars
facts: Olympus Mons rises about 22 km above the datum: the tallest volcano known.
Valles Marineris is about 4,000 km long and up to 7 km deep.
Surface pressure averages about 6 mbar, under 1 % of Earth's.
Its sol is 24 h 39 min long.

items.name: Phobos
facts: It orbits Mars faster than Mars turns, so it rises in the west.
Tides pull it down by about 2 m per century; it will break up or hit Mars in about 30–50 million years.
Stickney crater is 9 km wide on a moon about 22 km across.

items.name: Deimos
facts: About 12 km across, one of the smallest moons known.
From Mars it looks like a bright star, not a disc.
Its orbit, at 23,460 km, is just outside synchronous orbit, so it slowly moves away.

items.name: Ceres
facts: The largest body in the asteroid belt and a dwarf planet: about 39 % of the belt's mass.
Dawn found bright salt deposits (sodium carbonate) in Occator crater.
It may hold a layer of brine deep under its crust.
Discovered by Giuseppe Piazzi on 1 January 1801.

items.name: Vesta
facts: The brightest asteroid; it can be seen with the naked eye from Earth.
Rheasilvia, an impact basin at its south pole, is about 500 km wide, and its central peak is about 20 km high.
Many meteorites found on Earth (the HED meteorites) came from Vesta.

items.name: Pallas
facts: Its orbit is tilted about 35° to the ecliptic, so it is hard to reach.
The third-largest object in the belt, about 510 km across.

items.name: Psyche
facts: A metal-rich asteroid, possibly an exposed core of a shattered protoplanet.
NASA's Psyche spacecraft launched in October 2023 and arrives in 2029.

items.name: Eros
facts: NEAR Shoemaker was the first spacecraft to orbit an asteroid (2000) and to land on one (Eros, 2001).
A near-Earth asteroid, about 34 × 11 × 11 km.

items.name: Itokawa
facts: Hayabusa brought grains of it back to Earth in 2010: the first asteroid sample return.
A rubble pile about 535 m long, shaped like a sea otter.

items.name: Bennu
facts: OSIRIS-REx brought 121.6 g of it to Earth in September 2023.
Its surface is so loose that the sampling arm sank into it as if into a ball pit.

items.name: Ryugu
facts: Hayabusa2 returned 5.4 g of it in December 2020.
A carbon-rich, spinning-top-shaped rubble pile about 900 m across.

items.name: Jupiter
facts: More than twice the mass of all the other planets together.
The Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth, observed since at least 1831.
Its magnetic field traps radiation that kills unshielded electronics near Io and Europa.
A day lasts about 9 h 55 min: the shortest of any planet.

items.name: Io
facts: The most volcanic body known, with about 400 active volcanoes.
Tidal heating from its resonance with Europa and Ganymede melts its interior.
Io, Europa and Ganymede orbit in a 1:2:4 Laplace resonance.

items.name: Europa
facts: An ocean of liquid water, perhaps 60–150 km deep, lies under its ice shell.
Its ocean may hold about twice the water of Earth's oceans.
Europa Clipper launched in October 2024 to study it.

items.name: Ganymede
facts: The largest moon in the solar system, bigger than Mercury.
The only moon with its own magnetic field.
It likely has a salty ocean between layers of ice.

items.name: Callisto
facts: The most heavily cratered surface in the solar system.
It sits outside Jupiter's main radiation belts, so it is the safest large Jovian moon for crews.

items.name: Amalthea
facts: A small red moon so porous it may be a rubble pile of ice and rock.
It gives off more heat than it receives from the Sun.

items.name: Himalia
facts: The largest of Jupiter's irregular moons, about 140 km across.
Likely a captured asteroid.

items.name: Saturn
facts: Its mean density is less than that of water.
Its main rings span about 280,000 km but are mostly only about 10 m thick.
Winds at its equator reach about 1,800 km/h.

items.name: Mimas
facts: Herschel crater is about 139 km wide on a moon 396 km across.
It clears the Cassini Division in Saturn's rings through a 2:1 resonance.

items.name: Enceladus
facts: Geysers at its south pole throw water from an underground ocean into space.
Its plumes feed Saturn's E ring.
Cassini found salts, silica and organic molecules in the plumes.

items.name: Tethys
facts: Mostly water ice, with a density close to 1 g/cm³.
Ithaca Chasma is a canyon about 2,000 km long.

items.name: Dione
facts: Its 'wispy terrain' is a network of bright ice cliffs.
It shares its orbit with two small Trojan moons, Helene and Polydeuces.

items.name: Rhea
facts: Saturn's second-largest moon, about 1,530 km across.
Mostly water ice with a little rock.

items.name: Titan
facts: The only moon with a thick atmosphere: surface pressure about 1.5 bar, mostly nitrogen.
It has lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane.
Huygens landed on it in January 2005.
Dragonfly, a nuclear-powered rotorcraft, is to launch to Titan in 2028.

items.name: Hyperion
facts: It tumbles chaotically: its spin is not predictable over long times.
Its spongy look comes from a very porous body.

items.name: Iapetus
facts: One side is as dark as coal and the other as bright as snow.
An equatorial ridge up to about 20 km high runs along much of its circumference.

items.name: Phoebe
facts: It orbits Saturn backwards and far out: likely a captured object from the outer solar system.
Dust from Phoebe forms a huge, faint ring around Saturn.

items.name: Uranus
facts: Its spin axis is tilted about 98°, so it rolls along its orbit.
Each pole gets about 42 years of daylight, then 42 years of night.
Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft to visit it (1986).

items.name: Miranda
facts: Verona Rupes may be the highest cliff in the solar system, about 20 km.
Its patchwork surface suggests it was heated and reshaped in the past.

items.name: Ariel
facts: The brightest of Uranus's large moons, with long rift valleys.

items.name: Umbriel
facts: The darkest of Uranus's large moons.

items.name: Titania
facts: Uranus's largest moon, about 1,580 km across.

items.name: Oberon
facts: The outermost large moon of Uranus, heavily cratered.

items.name: Neptune
facts: Found in 1846 from the math of its pull on Uranus, before anyone saw it.
Its winds are the fastest measured in the solar system, up to about 2,100 km/h.
One orbit takes 165 years: it completed its first orbit since discovery in 2011.

items.name: Triton
facts: It orbits Neptune backwards: almost certainly a captured Kuiper belt object.
Voyager 2 saw nitrogen geysers on it in 1989.
Its surface, at about −235 °C, is one of the coldest measured.

items.name: Nereid
facts: One of the most eccentric moon orbits known (e ≈ 0.75).

items.name: Proteus
facts: About as large as a body can be without being pulled round by its own gravity.
